text: My name is Robert Brennan.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm the CEO at OpenHands, and I want to talk to you a little bit today about sandboxing coding agents, why this is a really important pattern, and different ways to actually get this done.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A little bit about me.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Like I said, I'm the CEO of OpenHands, co-founded it a little over two years ago, really with the vision of bringing coding agents to the community, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Really giving software developers a say in the gigantic change that's happening to our jobs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we started OpenHands as an MIT licensed coding agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I would say now we've evolved really to a platform for running coding agents, everything from the harness to the infrastructure to the control plane to actually monitor these agents at scale.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A little bit about the history of AI-driven development and how we got to where we are today and, you know, where I think things are going in the future.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We really started with, like, code snippets being generated by a chatbot, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I remember the first time I typed in a ChatGPT, like, write a SQL query that does X and it just, like, one-shotted it and I was blown away.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It feels very antiquated today.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But, you know, my original workflow was a lot of, like, type in a ChatGPT, paste something into my IDE, hit enter, paste an error message back into ChatGPT, and it was pretty quick that I realized, like, hey, this is kind of dumb, I can just, like, wire some APIs together, and very quickly we got these AI-powered IDEs, stuff like Cursor and GitHub Copilot doing things like autocomplete, right, where now you have the context of the code base, you're not just generating code snippets inside of a chat window, you're actually modifying the code itself
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can see the variable names that are available there.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the AI gets a little bit smarter, a little bit more context aware.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then the big leap in like the beginning of 2024 was this leap to agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So AI that wasn't just writing code, but was actually running the code that it wrote, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Actually like looking at the error messages, Googling them, really doing that entire loop of development on top of the LLM.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that's kind of where we're at today.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I would say most developers today are still running something like Claude Code or OpenHands or Codex on their laptop as kind of a pair programmer model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They're manually prompting this thing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The leap that we're seeing organizations make over the course of 2026 is really to agents that run in the cloud.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is really where sandboxing comes into play.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One, because it needs a place to work in the cloud, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You need to give this agent a terminal, a file system, et cetera.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But two, because you're able to do a lot more once you've got these agents in the cloud, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And you need to make sure that they have access only to the things that they're allowed to access, because there's not necessarily going to be a human there to babysit them, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Going forward from there, I think the more we get agents running in the cloud, running autonomously, running in response to events coming out of systems like GitHub and Datadog and Slack, rather than being manually prompted, you're going to get these interactions between agents where one agent opens a PR, another's doing code review, and they're going back and forth.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We see these multi-agent teams emerging.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then I think the endgame is really this full SDLC automation where humans aren't even looking at the source code anymore.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But the thing I really want to talk today about is how do we make this leap from number three, where we're running agents on our machine, to number four, where we've got agents running in the cloud.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So let's talk a little bit about running locally.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Who here runs Claude Code on their laptop or Codex or OpenHand, some local agent?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: All right.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Fewer than I would expect.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Keep your hand raised if you use dangerously skipped permissions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Yeah, okay.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I have more hands than before.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is the big tradeoff when running agents locally, right, is you can either sit there and hit like yes, yes, yes, you're allowed to do that over and over again and babysit the agent while it works, or you can go into dangerously skip permissions mode and just like trust that the agent isn't going to delete a file you really care about or access your production database or anything like that, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So running locally, you are kind of limited by those two options.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And if you do run locally and you run with dangerously skipped permissions, the agent does have access to a lot of things, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It has access to your whole local file system, it has access to any secrets that are in your environment variables, it has access to any secrets that are in your home directory,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you're connected to like a production database or a production Kubernetes cluster, the agent can get in there.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It has access basically to everything that you have access to, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So super important that you either sit there and babysit it and watch what it's doing or you find a way to cut off its access and really only give it access to the things that it needs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is a paradigm that we actually know well from, you know, pre-agent security days is the principle of least privilege, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The idea is that both agents and humans should only have access to the things that they need in order to do their job, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the agent shouldn't have access to every secret on your system.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It shouldn't have access to every file on your system.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It should only have access to the GitHub repo that it's editing and maybe a couple secrets that it needs to access a local database, something like that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So it's important when we start to sandbox these agents that we're looking at what exactly does this agent need in order to do its job.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then we can create a sandbox that has just exactly those things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then we know that the blast radius of a prompt injection attack or the agent getting confused, anything that could go wrong, like we limit the blast radius by limiting how much the agent has access to.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the first strategy that folks tend to experiment with is running inside of Docker containers on their laptop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is actually the way we originally launched OpenHands was as an interface where every time you started a new conversation with the agent, we'd spin up a brand new Docker container, the agent would get its own container.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this works really nicely for several things, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One, it's ephemeral, so the agent can do kind of whatever it wants.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If it runs RMRF slash and deletes everything, you just kill the container and start again, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's a very nice, the agent can just kind of run wild.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You don't have to worry too much about what it's going to do.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And because it's running locally on your laptop, you can also mount in things selectively from your local file system, you know, like a Git repo.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can mount ports so that the agent can run out an application and you can view it in your browser.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can mount specific secrets and environment variables for the agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can have MCP servers either running locally on your laptop or inside the Docker container.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it's nice because the agent is still working with like your local copy of the code, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's similar to how you're used to working where you've got like a copy of the code on your workstation and instead of you editing it, the agent's editing it now and you're deciding when to git push and all that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But this doesn't really scale very well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's only so many Docker containers you can get running on a laptop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Your laptop can't listen for events coming out of Slack and Datadog, et cetera.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is pretty limited in terms of what you can do here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The next strategy we see folks taking is starting to like glue together Claude Code and GitHub Actions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is definitely different from like running Docker containers in your computer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now you're no longer working with your local copy of the code base.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You're now, you know, having this agent inside of like an ephemeral environment somewhere inside of GitHub Actions, cloning the repo, doing stuff, you know, and then like shipping it off and then everything goes away once that action spins down.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But what's nice is that you can run as many GitHub Actions as you're willing to pay for.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It has built-in support for things like a secrets registry.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you get these nice isolated environments.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And what's really cool is now you can run them on a schedule.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can just have a GitHub Action that spins up an agent every Monday morning at 9 a.m. and updates your dependencies.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can have a GitHub Action that any time a PR gets opened is gonna use an agent to do code review.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you can start to get some automation in place now that the agents are off your laptop and in the cloud.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But you're locked into GitHub Actions, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is a proprietary standard.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You're not gonna be able to really port this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's only able to respond to events coming out of GitHub, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can't respond to like a Slack web hook or a Datadog web hook.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you're kind of limited in terms of what you can do by just like gluing things together with GitHub Actions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The next strategy we saw folks take was kind of in the OpenClaw craze, where you actually get a separate computer, you know, a virtual machine in the cloud, or maybe a Mac Mini, and just put all your agents on that, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is different from GitHub Actions, and now you've got a long-lived environment.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You've got persistence, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Which is good and bad, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Your agents can modify the system and know it's going to be that way again when they run, you know, two days from now.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But your machine could get into a bad state as well, and you might have to go and debug and figure out what's going on.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Again, just like in GitHub Actions, you can run agents on a schedule.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, if you're running on a VM, you can actually listen for web hooks coming in from Twilio.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you want to listen for text messages from Slack, you can listen for incidents coming out of Datadog, events coming out of GitHub.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you get agents running automatically now.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But you still have this principle of least privilege problem, right, where all of your agents are now co-located in this virtual machine, and they all have access to the same stuff.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you might have a code review agent in there alongside a Datadog incident triage bot, and the code review agent now for some reason has accessed the Datadog, and there's just a lot more possibility for things to go wrong, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The code review bot can even edit the memory for the Datadog bot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This co-locating problem quickly runs into issues where agents have access to way more than they necessarily need in order to do their job.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So way more opportunities for things to go wrong when all these agents are bumping into each other.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The fourth and really the most robust strategy here, I would say, is to use Kubernetes or some other highly scalable environment that's ephemeral, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And now you're getting, with Kubernetes, say, you get a pod for every agent session you want to run.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It spins up, the agent runs, does its work,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Maybe working on a local copy of the repo.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then it spins down and all that environment goes away.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The agent has opened up a pull request or something like that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is really nice because you don't have to worry about the long-term state of this thing the way you do with a VM.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You don't have to worry about it getting into a bad state because every time an agent runs, you're basically killing the environment and starting fresh.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And you get like an infinite amount of scale, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You have cloud scale at this point.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can run as many agents as you want as long as you're, again, willing to pay for the memory and CPU to run them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And again, because it's Kubernetes, it's running in the cloud,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can run things on a schedule using cron jobs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can run things in response to HTTP events coming out of Slack and GitHub and JIRA.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can basically run agents fully automatically.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A little kind of like quick comparison here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'll just go down the things that I look at when I'm comparing these different strategies.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One is, is it local or is it remote, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Is it on your laptop working with your copy of the code base or is it running somewhere else that has to like clone in the code itself or with its own copy?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Those are two very different ways of working.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What kind of scale can you get out of this thing, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you're running locally on your laptop, you can maybe run ones of agents before things start getting uncomfortable.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you're in Kubernetes, you can run thousands.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Level of isolation, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you're not running, if you're running like dangerously skipped permissions on your laptop, you've got nothing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you've got all your agents like co-located in a VM, they're separated from your environment, but they can still step on each other's toes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But something like Kubernetes, every agent has its own workspace, you know, it's doing its own thing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Level of persistence.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can always get some persistence by saving files out or writing to external systems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But when you're working on your laptop or you're working in a VM, you do get just persistence by default.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That system is long-lived.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then what kinds of triggers can actually cause these agents to run?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You're typing in a prompt.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Once you get into the cloud, you can start to run things on a schedule or run things in response to events.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00
